initial_observation.encounter_context: presented from jail with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and focal peritonitis 4 days after being struck multiple times in the abdomen
initial_observation.chief_complaint: worsening abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and focal peritonitis; initial WBC was 38.4 × 10^9/L, platelet count was 691 × 10^9/L
presenting_symptoms: focal peritonitis (upper abdominal tenderness with rebound and guarding)
vague abdominal pain for 2 months prior

evidence_items.source_text: Initial WBC was 38.4 × 109/L, PC was 691 × 109/L, and lipase was 55 U/L.
A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen demonstrated a hematoma encasing the distal pancreas, abutting the stomach and colon, with a small amount of hemoperitoneum (Fig. 1).

Given the concern for bowel injury, the patient was taken for emergent exploratory laparotomy. The surgery revealed a nearly severed distal pancreas and a devascularized colon, necessitating a distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and colonic resection with primary anastomosis.
Leukocytosis peaked at 69.6 × 109/L on POD-9 and thrombocytosis peaked at 2293 × 109/L on POD-12.
Despite sepsis workup, including repeat CT with oral and intravenous contrast, no source of infection or contrast leak was identified. His procalcitonin was consistently low (0.11–0.13 ng/mL).
Peripheral blood smear demonstrated severe leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, but no circulating blasts.
Subsequent workup included molecular testing for Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), calreticulin (CALR), and myeloproliferative leukemia virus oncogene (MPL), which were negative.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of BCR–ABL was positive.

A subsequent bone marrow biopsy demonstrated slightly hypercellular marrow (70%) with evidence of trilineage hematopoiesis, mild myeloid hyperplasia, mild megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and molecular evidence of BCR/ABL + fusion, consistent with CML, chronic phase.
The fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis detected BCR–ABL1 fusions in 91.5% of the nuclei examined, confirming the presence of the t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome).
Initial treatment included hydroxyurea, with transition to imatinib (400 mg daily).

After initiation of CML treatment, the patient’s hospital course was further complicated by intra-abdominal fluid collections, necessitating medical therapy via cefepime, metronidazole, and micafungin, as well as direct drainage by interventional radiology.
He was then discharged to an outside facility with WBC of 11.6 × 109/L and PC of 932 × 109/L.
